name: Gay-Lussac's Law
statement: At constant volume, a gas's pressure rises in proportion to its absolute temperature.
statementAccent: rises in proportion to its absolute temperature
meaning: Heat a gas trapped in a rigid, sealed container and its pressure climbs in lockstep with temperature — double the absolute temperature and the pressure doubles. Because the volume cannot change, all the added molecular energy shows up as increased pressure.
mechanism: In a rigid container, raising the temperature makes molecules move faster, so they strike the walls both more often and with greater force. Pressure is the force per unit area of those collisions, and with the volume fixed there is no room to expand and relieve it, so the pressure rises. The relationship is linear only against absolute temperature, measured from absolute zero.

examples.text: An aerosol can is a rigid sealed vessel; left in a hot car or thrown in a fire, its internal pressure rises with temperature until it can rupture — the reason for 'do not incinerate' warnings.
Heating the trapped steam in a near-fixed volume raises its pressure, which raises the boiling point and cooks food faster, with a relief valve capping the rise.
After hard driving or on a hot day, the gas in a tyre warms and, at roughly fixed volume, its measured pressure climbs — why the advice is to check pressures when tyres are cold.

variants.name: Amontons's law
variants.text: The same pressure-temperature relationship under its historically prior name, after Guillaume Amontons, who established it around 1700 — a century before Gay-Lussac.

variants.name: The law of combining volumes
variants.text: A completely different law also called 'Gay-Lussac's law': gases reacting chemically do so in volume ratios of small whole numbers, announced in 1808 — a frequent source of confusion.

whyItMatters: It completes the trio of simple gas laws linking pressure, volume, and temperature, and it explains a family of everyday hazards and devices, from bursting cans to pressure cookers. It is also a lesson in nomenclature: the single label 'Gay-Lussac's law' is attached to three different things, so precision about which one is meant matters.

working.lead: Work in kelvin at fixed volume
working.text: the proportionality holds only for absolute temperature in a rigid container of fixed gas; convert to kelvin and keep the volume constant.
distinguish the pressure-temperature law here from the law of combining volumes and from Charles's volume-temperature law, all of which share the name.
sealed vessels can develop dangerous pressures when heated; design in relief and heed temperature limits.

limits: Like its siblings it holds only for an ideal gas, at constant volume and fixed amount, and requires absolute temperature. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, near condensation, where intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume matter. Its name is genuinely ambiguous — it denotes this pressure-temperature law (better called Amontons's law), the 1808 law of combining volumes, and sometimes the volume-temperature law now called Charles's law — so the label alone under-specifies which relationship is meant.
misreadings: It is not the only 'Gay-Lussac's law', and it is arguably better named for Amontons, who found it a century earlier. It is also not exact for real gases, and it applies strictly at constant volume — confusing it with Charles's constant-pressure law or the law of combining volumes is the common error.
origin: The pressure-temperature relationship was established empirically by Guillaume Amontons around 1700 and measured more precisely across several gases by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac in the early 1800s, whose name it conventionally carries. It was later explained by kinetic theory and absorbed into the ideal gas law.
